title: Welding processes and weld defects
goals: Tell MMA, MIG/MAG, TIG and submerged arc apart, and say where each suits
Work out a weld's heat input from volts, amps and travel speed
Name the common weld imperfections, their causes, and which are most serious
Say why hydrogen cracking means waiting before the final inspection
Pick an NDT method for a given weld imperfection
summary:
**Arc welding** melts the joint with an electric arc and protects the molten pool from the air. The processes (with their ISO 4063 numbers):

- **MMA** (stick, 111): a flux-coated electrode; the flux makes gas and slag. Simple, portable, all positions, outdoors; slow, and slag to chip off.
- **MIG/MAG** (131/135): wire fed through the torch, shielded by gas: inert (argon) for **MIG** on aluminium, active (argon with CO₂) for **MAG** on steel. Fast and the most used; draughts blow the gas away.
- **TIG** (141): a tungsten electrode that does not melt, separate filler, argon. Slow, clean, precise: thin metal, stainless, root runs.
- **Submerged arc** (121): automatic, under a blanket of granular flux. Deep, fast, thick plate, flat position.

**Heat input** $Q = \frac{k \times V \times I \times 60}{1000 \times S}$ kJ/mm, with S the travel speed in mm/min and k the process's thermal efficiency (EN 1011-1: SAW 1.0; MMA and MIG/MAG 0.8; TIG 0.6). Too low: lack of fusion, hard brittle zones; too high: big grains, distortion, lost toughness. The WPS sets the range.

**Imperfections** (EN ISO 6520-1), judged against quality levels in EN ISO 5817 (B stringent, C, D moderate):

- **Planar**, the most serious: **cracks**, **lack of fusion**, **incomplete penetration**. Sharp edges grow under load. Best found by **UT** (inside) or **MT/PT** (surface).
- **Volumetric**: **porosity** (gas: damp, dirt, lost shielding), **slag inclusions** (poor cleaning between runs). Best shown by **RT**.
- **Shape**: undercut, overlap, excess metal, misalignment. Found by **VT**.

**Hydrogen cracking** (cold cracking) needs hydrogen, a hard heat-affected zone (HAZ) and stress. It can appear hours to days after welding, so final NDT waits (often 16 to 48 hours). Prevent it with dry low-hydrogen consumables and preheat.

formulas.name: Heat input
formulas.says: The arc's power (volts × amps), times the share that reaches the joint, spread over how much weld is laid down per second.
symbols: the process's thermal efficiency (SAW 1.0; MMA, MIG/MAG 0.8; TIG 0.6)
formulas.example: MAG at 25 V, 200 A, 300 mm/min: $\frac{0.8 \times 25 \times 200 \times 60}{1000 \times 300} = 0.8$ kJ/mm.

bench.task: Ask to see a Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) for a job at work, and read it against this lesson. Reading only.
check: Find the process number (111, 135, 141…) and the shielding gas
Find the current, voltage and travel speed ranges and work out the heat input range
Find any preheat and the consumable's hydrogen class
Find the NDT required and any hold time before it

cards.q: MAG welding outside on a windy day leaves welds full of small round holes. What has gone wrong?
options: The wind blew the shielding gas away
The current was set too low
The wire is the wrong diameter
The steel is too thick for MAG
cards.why: MAG relies on a gas shield over the pool. A draught strips it away, the molten metal picks up air, and gas comes out as it freezes: porosity. Screens, or MMA or flux-cored wire (whose flux makes its own shield), suit windy sites.

cards.title: Four arc processes
cards.body:
All arc welding melts the joint with an electric arc and **shields** the molten pool from the air. They differ in how:

- **MMA** (stick): a flux-coated rod; the flux burns to gas and slag. Simple, portable, all positions.
- **MIG/MAG**: wire fed through the torch with a **shielding gas**. Fast; most welding is done this way.
- **TIG**: a **tungsten** electrode that does not melt; filler added by hand; argon gas. Slow, clean, precise.
- **Submerged arc**: automatic, under a heap of granular **flux**. Thick plate, fast, flat position.
cards.more:
Air is the enemy: oxygen and nitrogen in molten steel make it porous and brittle. Each process keeps the air out its own way.

MMA brings its shield on the rod: the coating melts into gas and a slag crust. That makes it robust outdoors, but every run leaves slag to chip off.

MIG/MAG brings it in a gas bottle: no slag, and the wire never needs changing mid-run, so it is quick. A breeze is its weakness.

TIG's tungsten carries the arc but does not melt, so heat and filler are controlled separately: beautiful welds on thin stainless and aluminium, and root runs on pipe, but slow.

Submerged arc buries the arc under flux: no light, no spatter, very deep and fast, ideal for long seams on thick plate.

cards.q: Match each process with its description.
pairs: A flux-coated electrode, all positions, outdoors
Wire fed through the torch, with a shielding gas
Tungsten electrode, separate filler, very controllable
Automatic, under a blanket of granular flux
cards.why: They differ in how the arc is shielded and how filler is added.

cards.title: MIG or MAG: the gas matters
cards.body:
The same torch does both; the gas is the difference.

- **MIG** (metal inert gas, 131): **argon** (or argon with helium). Inert gases do not react: used on **aluminium**, copper and other non-ferrous metals.
- **MAG** (metal active gas, 135): argon with some **CO₂** (and sometimes oxygen). The active part steadies the arc and improves penetration on **steel**.

**Flux-cored** wire (136) has flux inside the wire, for deeper welds and better tolerance of draughts.
cards.more:
On steel, pure argon gives a wandering arc and narrow, finger-like penetration; a little CO₂ or oxygen makes the arc behave and the weld wet out. A common shop mix is argon with 15–20% CO₂.

On aluminium, that oxygen would make oxide in the weld, so it is pure argon. Aluminium also needs a softer wire feed and a push angle.

In everyday talk 'MIG' is used for both; on a WPS the process number (131 or 135) says which.

cards.q: Which shielding gas suits MIG welding of an aluminium frame?
options: Pure argon
Argon with 20% CO₂
Pure CO₂
Compressed air
cards.why: Aluminium needs an inert gas: argon (or argon–helium). CO₂ is active and would oxidise the aluminium; argon–CO₂ mixes are for steel (MAG).

cards.title: Heat input
cards.body:
How much heat goes into each millimetre of weld affects its strength and toughness:

$$Q = \frac{k \times V \times I \times 60}{1000 \times S}$$

$Q$ in kJ/mm; $V$ volts and $I$ amps of the arc; $S$ the travel speed in mm/min; $k$ the share of the arc's heat that reaches the joint (EN 1011-1: submerged arc 1.0, MMA and MIG/MAG 0.8, TIG 0.6).

Too **low**: lack of fusion and a hard, crack-prone heat-affected zone. Too **high**: coarse grains, lost toughness, distortion. The **WPS** gives the range.
cards.more:
Volts times amps is the arc's power in watts: 25 V at 200 A is 5000 W, 5 kJ every second. Times 0.8 for what reaches the work: 4 kJ a second.

At 300 mm/min the torch covers 5 mm a second. So each millimetre gets $4 \div 5 = 0.8$ kJ.

The ×60 and ÷1000 in the formula are just that unit change: mm/min to mm/s, and J to kJ.

Weld slower and each millimetre gets more heat; turn the current up, likewise. Welders tend to slow down on awkward joints, and that is how heat input drifts above the WPS.

cards.q: A MAG weld runs at {volts} V and {amps} A, travelling at {spd} mm/min. Thermal efficiency 0.8. What is the heat input?
cards.why: Arc power × efficiency, divided by the travel speed. The 60 turns mm/min into mm/s; the 1000 turns J into kJ.
cards.hint: Volts × amps × 0.8 × 60, all over 1000 × the travel speed.

cards.title: Imperfections: planar ones matter most
cards.body:
Standards call them **imperfections**; whether one is a **defect** depends on the quality level asked for (EN ISO 5817: B stringent, C, D moderate).

- **Planar**: **cracks**, **lack of fusion** (the weld did not melt into the side or root), **incomplete penetration**. Flat with sharp edges: they grow under load and fatigue. The most serious.
- **Volumetric**: **porosity** (gas pores), **slag inclusions**. Rounded; usually less harmful in small amounts.
- **Shape**: **undercut** (a groove melted into the parent metal at the toe), **overlap**, excess metal, misalignment.
cards.more:
Think of tearing paper. A small round hole in a sheet barely weakens it: the tear has to start somewhere. A cut with a sharp end is where a tear starts at once. Cracks and lack of fusion are cuts; pores are holes.

So EN ISO 5817 allows a little scattered porosity even at its strictest level, but no cracks at any level, and little or no lack of fusion.

Undercut is a shape fault, but it is a notch at the weld toe, exactly where fatigue cracks like to start, so on cyclically loaded parts it matters too.

cards.q: Which weld imperfections are usually the most serious?
options: Cracks and lack of fusion
A few small, scattered gas pores
Spatter left on the parent plate
A weld cap a little too high
cards.why: Planar imperfections have sharp edges that concentrate stress and grow under load. Small rounded pores are far less harmful, and spatter and a slightly high cap are cosmetic in most work.

cards.title: Causes you can control
cards.body:
- **Porosity**: gas in the pool: damp or dirty plate or consumables, oil, paint, lost gas shield (draughts, flow too low or far too high), a leaking hose.
- **Slag inclusions**: slag left between runs (MMA, flux-cored) because it was not cleaned off, or trapped by poor technique.
- **Lack of fusion**: too little heat (current low, speed high), wrong torch angle, or welding onto a cold or dirty face.
- **Undercut**: too much current or too long an arc, too fast, or the wrong angle.
- **Incomplete penetration**: root gap too small, root face too thick, current too low.
cards.more:
Most imperfections are a setting or a habit, which is why a Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) fixes the settings and welders are qualified to it (EN ISO 9606-1).

A quick diagnosis guide: holes, look at the gas and the cleanliness. Black lines between runs on a radiograph, look at the interpass cleaning. A UT indication along the fusion face, look at heat and angle. A groove at the toe, look at current and arc length.

MIG/MAG's 'cold lap' (lack of fusion) is the classic: the bead looks fine on top but sat on the plate without melting into it, because the settings were too cold for the thickness.

cards.q: Match each imperfection with a likely cause.
pairs: Damp consumables or lost gas shield
Slag not cleaned off between runs
Too little heat, or the wrong torch angle
Too much current or too long an arc
cards.why: Each imperfection points back to a setting or a habit.

cards.title: Hydrogen cracking, and why NDT waits
cards.body:
**Hydrogen cracking** (cold cracking) happens in the **heat-affected zone** (HAZ) beside the weld when three things meet: **hydrogen** in the weld, a **hard** microstructure (hardenable steels, thick sections cooling fast) and **stress**.

It can appear **hours or even days** after welding. So final NDT on susceptible joints waits for a **hold time** (often 16 to 48 hours).

Prevention: **dry, low-hydrogen** consumables (baked electrodes, kept in a quiver), **preheat** to slow the cooling, clean joints, and enough heat input.
cards.more:
Hydrogen gets in from damp flux, moisture, oil or rust, dissolves in the hot weld metal, then slowly diffuses into the HAZ as it cools. If the HAZ has formed hard, brittle structure, the hydrogen gathers at tiny defects and the residual stress from welding pulls them open into cracks.

It is sneaky: a weld can pass UT an hour after welding and crack overnight. That is why procedures for thick or high-strength steel say how long to wait before the inspection that counts.

Preheat (warming the joint first, say to 100 °C) slows the cooling, so the HAZ is softer, and gives the hydrogen time to escape.

cards.q: A procedure says final UT of a thick high-strength steel weld must wait 48 hours after welding. Why?
options: Hydrogen cracks can form hours or days later
The weld must cool to room temperature first
Couplant will not stick to fresh weld metal
The steel's sound velocity settles over two days
cards.why: Hydrogen cracking is delayed: it needs time for hydrogen to diffuse into the hard HAZ. Testing too soon could pass a weld that cracks later.

cards.q: A TIG root run: 12 V, 110 A, 80 mm/min. Is it inside a WPS range of 0.4 to 0.8 kJ/mm?

steps.ask: The share reaching the joint (TIG, k = 0.6).

cards.why: Power, efficiency, speed, divide. TIG's k of 0.6 is lower than MAG's 0.8 because more of its heat is lost to the surroundings.

cards.q: A TIG weld (k = 0.6) runs at {volts} V, {amps} A and {spd} mm/min. What is the heat input?
cards.why: The same formula, with TIG's thermal efficiency of 0.6.

cards.q: A welder's notes on a MAG job that came out porous. One line is the most likely cause. Which?
lines: Plate cleaned back to bright metal with a flap disc
Wire: dry, from a sealed reel
Welded beside the open roller-shutter door, fan running behind me
Current and voltage as the WPS
cards.fix: Screen the weld area from draughts (or close the door and stop the fan)
cards.why: Everything else is as it should be; a draught across the torch strips the gas shield. Porosity points first to gas cover and cleanliness.

cards.q: Match each imperfection with the NDT method best suited to find it.
pairs: Lack of sidewall fusion inside a thick butt weld
Scattered porosity through a butt weld
A toe crack on a steel fillet weld
cards.why: Planar and internal: UT. Volumetric: RT. Surface on steel: MT. Shape: the eye and a gauge.

cards.q: Why is MMA still used on construction sites, though MAG is faster?
options: It needs no gas bottle and copes with wind
It gives the cleanest welds of any process
It needs no welder qualification
It works only on thin sheet
cards.why: The flux coating makes its own shield, so there is no gas to blow away and no bottle to carry. It is simple and works in all positions. The cost is speed and slag removal.

cards.q: A WPS limits MAG heat input to {qmax} kJ/mm. At {volts} V and {amps} A (k = 0.8), what is the slowest travel speed allowed, in mm/min?
cards.why: Turn the heat-input formula round for the speed. Slower than this puts more heat into each millimetre than the WPS allows.
cards.hint: Swap Q and S: $S = \frac{k V I \times 60}{1000\,Q}$.

cards.q: Why is a thick, high-strength steel joint preheated before welding?
options: To slow the cooling, so the HAZ is softer and hydrogen escapes
To make the steel easier to cut to shape
To burn off the mill scale for appearance
To raise the arc voltage for the same current
cards.why: Fast cooling of a thick, hardenable section makes a hard HAZ that hydrogen cracking loves. Preheat slows the cooling and gives hydrogen time to diffuse out.

cards.q: Submerged arc welding at {volts} V, {amps} A and {spd} mm/min. What is the heat input?
cards.why: Same formula, but submerged arc's k is 1.0: the flux blanket keeps almost all the heat in the joint. Using MAG's 0.8 here is the slip.

cards.q: Radiography of a butt weld shows clean film, but UT from the side finds a strong indication along one fusion face. What is it most likely to be?
options: Lack of sidewall fusion
Scattered porosity
Excess weld metal
Spatter on the surface
cards.why: A flat imperfection along the fusion face is planar: RT can miss it unless the beam runs along it, while an angle probe meets it square on. Porosity would show on the film.

cards.q: Which process suits a neat root run on thin-walled stainless steel pipe?
options: TIG
Submerged arc
MMA with a 5 mm rod
Flux-cored MAG at high current
cards.why: TIG separates heat from filler, so the welder can control a thin root precisely. Submerged arc is for thick, flat seams; big MMA rods and high-current flux-cored would burn through thin wall.

cards.q: A MIG weld on aluminium shows heavy porosity. Which check comes first?
options: The gas: argon flowing, no draught, no leak
The weld's tensile strength
The paint system to be applied
The plate's Charpy toughness
cards.why: Porosity is gas in the pool: check the shield first (flow, draughts, hose leaks), then cleanliness (aluminium oxide and grease), then damp wire.

cards.q: MAG (k = 0.8) at {volts} V, {amps} A, {spd} mm/min. Heat input?
cards.why: Arc power × efficiency ÷ travel speed, in kJ per mm.

cards.q: Sort each imperfection.
